newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland says Russia hatching security plan at OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Poland says Russia hatching security plan at OSCE.

text.p: Russia is likely to propose a plan for European security as an alternative to NATO enlargement during the December OSCE summit in Lisbon, Poland's Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said on Thursday.
"We can expect the Russian Federation will launch an offensive with a concept proposing a certain alternative to the enlargement of NATO," Rosati told a news conference.

He said Poland did not know exactly what it would consist of, but added: "From some elements of statements by Russian government representatives it...concerns giving a bigger role to the OSCE (Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe)."
He said Poland agreed with developing the OSCE but this could not replace the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
"There is no physical possibility another organisation with a similar character could arise parallel to NATO," he said.
Poland, to be represented in Lisbon by President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Rosati, sees NATO entry as a top priority.

It is sure of being in the first rank of new members alongside the Czechs and Hungarians, and has been heartened by freshly re-elected U.S. President Bill Clinton's campaign statement that enlargement should happen by 1999.
Rosati said he was sure that by then there would be enough supporters in the U.S. Senate -- two-thirds of its members -- for Poland's admission to NATO to be ratified there.
But Russia's objections to the inclusion of Poland in NATO have troubled Warsaw's relations with Moscow, which Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz will visit next week.
Rosati said internal affairs in Russia, such as election campaigns or the health of its leader President Boris Yeltsin, should not be allowed to influence the process of admitting new states to NATO.

Poland, which was dominated by the former Soviet Union, stresses that NATO enlargement is not aimed against Moscow and Rosati said Warsaw did not oppose the conclusion of a strategic partnership between NATO and Russia.
But he said this should not be a condition of NATO's growth, adding that Poland would rather it was concluded after the pact's enlargement and Poland should take part in its negotiation.
Rosati said there was some evolution of Russian views on NATO and he otherwise viewed ties "positively and highly".

He said that during Cimoszewicz's visit, the countries were expected to sign agreements including a long-negotiated deal on settlement of mutual trade debts left over from the 1980s, when they belonged to the now defunct Comecon bloc.
During a visit to Poland last month, Russian deputy Prime Minister Oleg Davydov suggested moves towards opening a free trade zone between the two countries.

Asked to comment, Rosati said that while Poland favoured easing trade barriers, its priority was its assocation agreement with the European Union, which it also aims to join quickly, and other trade decisions were subject to this.
